chapter_theme: The end of the Arasiyal sarukkam: the king's young daughter is shown to the crowd and adorned, the city's festival darkens the sun, the prince enters the bride's chamber, is crowned beside her, gives her father the Vidyadhara realm and sinks into joy and wealth.

cast.role: an unnamed speaker who calls the onlookers to see the bride and groom
the kings gathered for the wedding
Tivittan, the dark-hued young prince, the groom

1531.reading: A voice calls the onlookers to look at the bride: her lotus-red eyes, long hands, coral mouth, lotus-scented feet and the jewelled chest, shining as the lotus lady praises her.
1531.nuance: The speaker is not named; the reading of the lotus (தாமரை) as Lakshmi in line 4 is read from பாராட்ட and the lotus-maiden, and may be only the poet's image.

1532.reading: The same voice shows the groom's glory: on a rutting elephant under a long jewelled umbrella, he shines like an autumn moon on a mountain beneath white cloud, with a red-lotus mouth and a garland.
1532.nuance: Line 4 is garbled in the edition (வருநனலர் தாரா ன்மற்), so the last clause is held loosely.
1532.event: A speaker presents the groom, riding an elephant under the royal umbrella, to the onlookers.

1533.reading: The voice goes on to praise the groom's body: red lips, lily-dark eyes, a moon-bright light, shoulders like a silver hill, dark hair falling to his back and the glow of his face under swinging earrings.
1533.nuance: That this is the groom and not the bride rests on the masculine shoulders and the sequence with 1532; no name is given.

1534.reading: The speaker says: let us go and see the king's young daughter, who sits among white-clad women praising her, like one inside a sky-travelling jewelled palace.
1534.nuance: ளிமானம் in line 3 is an edition slip for விமானம்.
1534.event: The speaker invites the crowd to go and see the king's daughter on her sky-palace.

1535.reading: In the jewelled palace with a crystal rim, the bride's own light shines back, and the poet says she is like a divine doll with hair dressed by hand and gem-set tresses, sitting on a golden couch.
1535.nuance: திக்ழ்ந்து in line 2 is a misprint for திகழ்ந்து; the doll-image is the poet's own and it makes her seem made, not born, which the verse does not say outright.

1536.reading: The speaker asks whether this is a mountain goddess, seeing the blue-gem eyes in her face like sapphires set in crystal and red lines drawn in a lotus.

1537.reading: Her eye-paint is not applied, kumkum lines and creeper-patterns are drawn on her breasts, and pearl strings are put on her; those who adorned her did not seem to try to make her waist exist at all.
1537.nuance: The last line plays on her waist being so slender that the adorners made no effort over it; the sense is held loosely.
1537.event: Her attendants adorn the bride with kumkum designs and pearls.

1538.reading: They tie around her a fragrant, gold-edged red cloth fine enough to move with a breath, and gem girdles over it, knowing her hips never leave her.
1538.nuance: The sense of line 4 (they know her hips never part from the cloth) is taken from the verb செய்தார் with அறிந்து and is not certain.
1538.event: Attendants dress the bride in a red cloth and gem girdles.

1539.reading: When the flower-spathe season spreads, the lute-voiced young women's sweet words and the mandara-scented bride's lotus-red feet make the speaker say this is surely a goddess.
1539.nuance: Line 1 (கந்தாரம் கொள வீக்கி) is obscure; it may mean a lute tuned in the gandhara mode, which would give the scene its music.

1540.reading: After showing many such sights, the young people watching them join the kings in throwing garlands and flowers on the king and spraying him with scented water, and the old city's joy begins.
1540.nuance: Whether the one showered (அரசர் தன்மேல்) is the groom or the old king is not fixed by the words.
1540.event: The kings and young people shower the king with garlands, flowers and scented water as the city festival opens.

1541.reading: Gold dust, scented sprays, golden flowers, incense smoke and golden banners darken the streets, so that the elephant-bearing king's elephant lights the way by its eyes.
1541.nuance: கம்பஞ்செய் யானையானை (line 4) is read as a shaking war-elephant and its rider; the lamp-eyed image is the poet's.
1541.event: The festival's smoke and decoration darken the streets until only the elephant's eyes seem to give light.

1542.reading: Maidens guard their own bright houses, with their brows as bows, glances as arrows, the white upper halls as ramparts and window-slits as the openings.
1542.nuance: The poem turns houses into forts and glances into arrows to say that the king cannot pass unwounded; the verse does not say who passes, which is taken from the sequence.
1542.event: Maidens at the windows shoot glances at the passing king.

1543.reading: Dancers, women armed with instruments, singers, praisers, and bowing men gather; the palace attendants surround the court in great numbers, so crowded that none can pass.
1543.nuance: கொற்றம் கொள்ளக் கூறுவார் (line 3) means those who pronounce blessings for victory.
1543.event: Entertainers and attendants crowd round the king in the palace city.

1544.reading: Flags and incense smoke fill the sky like cloud and dim the sun, which thinks it cannot shine here any more and sets on the western hill.
1544.nuance: The sun's withdrawal is an image of the festival outshining it; it is not claimed as an omen.
1544.event: The sun goes down, dimmed by the smoke of the festival.

1545.reading: The mountain-gem king enters his palace in the city, Payapati stands with his attendants, and the other kings go to their own palaces with the strong-armed Arukkan.
1545.nuance: The 'mountain-gem king' of line 1 and the Arukkan of line 4 are not named by standard titles; identifying them with Tivittan and Arukkakirthi is the sequence's best guess.
1545.event: The kings withdraw to their palaces at nightfall.

1546.reading: After the conch-white one enters his own tall palace, the red-bright, shark-ornamented prince goes with Fortune to meet him and enters the jewelled room of the Vidyadhara maiden, richer than Indra.
1546.nuance: வளைவண்ணன் (conch-coloured) is an epithet read as Vijayan, the white elder brother; செஞ்சுடர் மகரப் பூணான் is taken as Tivittan. Both are guesses from epithets.
1546.event: The prince enters the Vidyadhara bride's room.

1547.reading: At evening a drum proclaims that the auspicious queen's coronation will be at dawn, and the world's joy grows over the sea-bound earth as the lute-voiced one is made ready.
1547.nuance: The 'lute-voiced' woman (பாலையாழ் மழலையாள்) is the bride only by sequence.
1547.event: Heralds beat a drum announcing the bride's coronation as queen for the next morning.

1548.reading: Lamps, jewelled vessels and the bride's moon-like forehead chase the dark of the wedding night away, and the night slowly lets go.
1548.event: The night passes in the glow of lamps and the bride's face.

1549.reading: As the dark clears, the sun, grantor of the rising to the lotus Kamalini, arrives, and the discus-bearing prince goes with a kind heart to the golden palace of his dark-haired love.
1549.nuance: கமலினி is read as the lotus-bed that the sun favours and as a pun on the bride, not as a name; the prince as 'discus-bearer' is by epithet.
1549.event: The sun rises and the prince goes to the bride's golden palace.

1550.reading: Gem, gold, garlands and perfume are gathered as the Vidyadhara world and the earth and the sky seem one, and the sea-hued prince has her crowned queen with him.
1550.event: The sea-coloured prince crowns his bride queen beside him in a rich ceremony.

1551.reading: He honours the queen's father with a great gift, hands him the whole Vidyadhara realm on the silver mountain with its rights, and walks behind to send him off.
1551.nuance: The gift is a restoration of rule over Vidyadharas: the verse treats it as honour, not as a conquest being consolidated.
1551.event: The prince gives his father-in-law the Vidyadhara kingdom and sees him off.

1552.reading: With no enemy left, no direction left to subdue, a wife, the earth and Fortune, the gem-hued prince becomes intoxicated with joy.
1552.nuance: செருக்கிய களியன் (an elated, intoxicated one) uses a word that elsewhere can blame pride; here the poet does not.
1552.event: The prince, with no rival left, is filled with the pleasure of his fortune.

1553.reading: Two great treasures, guardians of the quarters, fall together at his feet, and the king, seeing the shining jewels, sinks into a sea of wealth.
1553.nuance: The 'two treasures' (நிதி இரண்டு) are read as the nidhis of Jain and Hindu tradition; the verse names no number beyond two.
1553.event: The two great treasures arrive at the king's feet and he is overwhelmed by wealth.

1554.reading: In the golden city of Vamana of the lotus feet, a festival and sacrifice fills the fertile city with delight.
1554.nuance: வேள்வி (sacrifice) is a Vedic word in a Jain work; whether it means a ritual or only a feast is not shown, and வாமன் is read as the king by epithet.
1554.event: The festival and sacrifice celebrate the king's fortune in the city.

links.note: 1541 darkens the streets with incense and gold; 1544 makes the sun give up and set.
links.teaches: The festival's smoke is first a lamp for the elephant's eyes, then the cause of the sun's flight: the poet builds one hyperbole across two verses.

links.note: 1547 announces the coronation at dawn; 1550 carries it out.
links.teaches: The announcement and the crowning make a promise and its keeping, so the festival is a prelude to the crowning, not merely its decoration.

links.note: 1381 has the Vidyadhara kings turn back from fated men; 1552 says no rival is left.
links.teaches: The Vidyadharas' flight from the battle is what leaves the prince without an enemy at the wedding; his joy is the victory's late fruit.

links.note: 1553 shows great treasure arriving and the king drowning in it; Kural 332 compares wealth's coming to a crowd gathering and its going to the crowd's scattering.
links.teaches: Read together, the epic shows only the gathering of the crowd, and the couplet supplies the scattering that the festival hides.

gains.a: The scene of arrival gains the knowledge that the sea of wealth is a crowd at a show that will break up.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king at the height of his fortune, not an anonymous owner, so the image is tested at its peak.

links.note: 1552 gives the prince's elation at fortune with no hint of its cause; Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time comes and leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar supplies a karmic account the epic withholds in these verses: his elation is for a fortune whose source and end are deeds, though the verse says no such thing.

gains.a: The prince's elation gains a limit that the poet does not state: the fortune is held by karma and not by his own act.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where wealth, wife and rule arrive together, so its claim is tested against a complete success.

source_issues: Every verse but 1552 to 1554 prints in 8 half-lines in the source and was joined into 4 lines by the build.
1537 line 3 had a stray pulli removed by the build.
1534 line 3 reads ளிமானத்தின் for விமானத்தின், and 1535 line 2 reads திக்ழ்ந்து for திகழ்ந்து.
1532 line 4 (வருநனலர் தாரா ன்மற்) is garbled in word division.
1545 and 1546 name the actors only by epithets (மணிவரை அரசன், வளைவண்ணன், மகரப் பூணான்); the identifications are by sequence.
